Marco Rubio, Secretary of State

Reykjavik, Iceland

Safnahúsið

Secretary of State Marco Rubio And Icelandic Foreign Minister Þorgerður Katrín Gunnarsdóttir At a Joint Press Availability

Remarks

October 6, 2026

FOREIGN MINISTER GUNNARSDÓTTIR:  (In Icelandic.)  Thank you all for being here.  I will not continue in Icelandic, my dear Marco, and thank you especially for visiting Iceland.  I think that demonstrates also very well our close connections and good relationship.  And it has actually been, from my point of view, a productive morning.  I would say so.  We started, as you know, at Hofdi House, where we first had the opportunity to hear about the historic summit back almost 40 years ago between President Ronald Reagan and Mikhail Gorbachev, and I hope you enjoyed our meeting in Hofdi.  I thought there’s a kind of special atmosphere there.

The Secretary and I, then we had an excellent bilateral meeting at Hofdi, and now, just now, we concluded a very good meeting with – here in Safnahusid with our prime minister here in Iceland, Kristrún Frostadóttir.  I would say throughout our discussions, they have been good and it has been very clear that Iceland and U.S., the United States of America, we enjoy a very good and strong and also enduring friendship.  We share a long history.  The U.S. was – as we have already mentioned, the U.S. was the first country to recognize the Republic of Iceland back in 1944.  We are both founding members of NATO 1949, and of course we have the valuable bilateral Defense Agreement between our two countries since 1951. 

And we are working closely together every day here in Iceland, especially to safeguard the security of the High North, North Atlantic, and the Arctic.  For us, being a credible and responsible ally, we take this role very seriously here in Iceland, especially when it comes to the U.S. and the whole of NATO.  And this is also very much and strongly reflected in our new policy – and actually the first one – policy and defense and security.  It also strongly emphasizes the very important relationship through defense and security with the U.S.  

With Iceland and the U.S. both being Arctic nations, the Secretary and I, we fully agreed on the need to work together to ensure a safe and secure Arctic region.  And I especially want to commend you, Marco, on how you have taken such a strong initiative to – in making the A7, Arctic 7 group, even more effective than it has been before.  And that matters for us here in Iceland a lot.

And we also discussed the agreement that has been found between the U.S., Greenland, and Denmark, and that is also hugely important for the region that we got this good agreement on Greenland.

As we discussed also in both our meetings now today, there are ample opportunities to deepen our economic and investment relations even further – for instance, in geothermal energy.  We discussed data centers, pharmaceuticals, as well as digital and other infrastructure.  And we also talked about the challenging global context, which is on our minds as Russia full-scale invasion in Ukraine – very brutal, very relentless.  And we touched on the dire situation in the Middle East and also we discussed our relations to China. 

But above all, the Secretary and I, we had productive and constructive discussions, conversation, and I think the message is very clear.  We are allies, we are friends, and we will continue working very closely to strengthen and deepen our good relationship. 

So over to you, dear Marco.

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, thank you for welcoming here – us here.  This is a place that many Americans visit.  I think the number that was shared with us as coming in and here today is over 700,000 Americans.  Our great ambassador, who’s only been here a couple months but is already doing a great job – so he’s going to get that up to a million American visitors over the next few years, but – with direct flights from multiple cities.  And now we see why people want to come here.  It’s a beautiful country, a wonderful people, the most peaceful country in the world.  It’s one of the safest countries in the world, a country that’s also blessed with abundance of energy that is renewable and self-sustaining. 

And so you have so many good things coming and going in your direction, and we’re so happy to be a close partner of yours, as we have been for a very long time.  We have tremendous respect for your – the people, and we have tremendous respect for the country and the role that it plays, and it has for a very long time.  I mean, for decades this nation in Iceland has occupied a critical strategic position for our collective security, and that remains true today more than ever before. 

And while the world’s focus drifted over the last 20 years, the reality is the geography is always important, and we’re seeing that come now to fruition.  The location of this country between the United States and Europe and the High North means that it sits at the – Iceland sits at the center of many of the questions surrounding the security and the defense of our shared region. 

And today those threats are growing, which is why this focus on the Arctic in general and Iceland in particular is so critical.  Our potential adversaries and real competitors already – and the predatory industries associated with them – are already acting as – against our interests.  And so it’s important that we continue to cooperate in the security realm the way we are doing and continue to do. 

Obviously I think one of the unique aspects of the country – in a positive way, I think – is that you don’t have a traditional military in the traditional sense of the word, but as – but you are a NATO member and you are a contributor to collective security, and you continue to contribute that critical role in our Alliance and share the burden of defending region.  And in practice, what that means and has meant for a very long time is you welcoming NATO Allies to come here and to operate jointly within Icelandic territory, and we want to continue to build upon that as a way to prevent conflict – not as a way to encourage conflict or provoke conflict, but prevent it. 

History teaches us that deterrence is the best prevention of violence and the best preventer of war.  And you play such – have played such a strategic role in the past and continue to play that now.  So since the Second World War, Iceland has allowed the U.S. military to project power and collectively working together, using your land, your air, your sea; giving us a critical outpost for monitoring clandestine behavior and deterring our adversaries from entering your sovereign territory and the sovereign territory of our mutual allies. 

This year marks the 75th anniversary of the 1951 U.S.-Iceland Defense Agreement.  And I’m proud to say that our military and our Icelandic partners continue to work together to secure this land and the waters that surround it.  Just last month, over 1,200 Americans participated along with our allies in the Northern Viking 2026 military exercise, something that’s occurred every year and will continue to occur.

And – but I want to talk a little bit beyond the military and security domain, because Iceland is not just an important security partner; it is a critical partner in our mutual economic interests for the foreseeable future.  Your landscapes, for example, have been the training ground for American astronauts since the Appollo program and continues to host training missions for the Artemis missions.  Your expertise in geothermal energy and biotechnology and marine industries, those present incredible opportunities for greater commercial and technological cooperation. 

We discussed that today and our efforts to perhaps – we are going to work now on building out a group of American industries and present them to investment opportunities that exist here, and likewise identify for your companies here investment opportunities that may exist in the United States.  That’s how you continue to build upon the economic bonds that lead to our shared prosperity and our mutual prosperity, so that’s important.  So today we discussed concrete ideas about how we can deepen cooperation in these fields and further strengthen our robust bilateral relationship to benefit our people. 

So I really look forward to – as I said, we had an opportunity to engage in Ankara earlier this year.  I told you I would be coming soon, and I’m here now and I’m happy to have come.  This is my first visit here in any capacity.  I believe – and we discussed this earlier – it’s probably the first bilateral visit by a secretary of state in a very long time.  I know Secretary Blinken had been here as part of a broader gathering earlier, but – and maybe we’ll be able to – but this, I think this is the first time a secretary of state comes in a long time in terms of a bilateral visit, and perhaps it won’t be the last one because of how much esteem we have for your country, for your government, for your people, and for the importance of this relationship.

So really, really happy to be here, really glad I came.  And now I know, just in the limited things I’ve gotten to see – because obviously there’s only so much you can see through the window of a hotel and the window of a car, but you can see why people fall in love with this country and you can see why Americans are fascinated by it, and we want to build upon that both in the tourism sector, in the economic sector, and in our enduring security cooperation.

So thank you for hosting me, for hosting us, and thank you for this opportunity to interact with you. 

FOREIGN MINISTER GUNNARSDÓTTIR:  Thank you, dear Marco.  And actually you saw – witnessed the Northern Lights yesterday.  You told me. 

SECRETARY RUBIO:  I did.  Which, as someone from Florida —

FOREIGN MINISTER GUNNARSDÓTTIR:  Yeah.  (Laughter.) 

SECRETARY RUBIO:  — I didn’t know if that was a UFO or what it was, but then I looked at it and I realized what it was pretty quickly.  It was very special. 

FOREIGN MINISTER GUNNARSDÓTTIR:  Thank you, Marco.  Who is going to conduct – yes, yeah. 

MODERATOR:  Thank you.  And we’ll take a few questions from the media now, starting with the Icelandic press.  Mr. Hallgrímur Indridason from RUV, the Icelandic broadcasting service.

QUESTION:  Thank you.  The first question from RUV:  In light of the deal that the U.S., Greenland, and Denmark made on Greenland defenses, which included buildup, like, in two more military bases in Greenland, are there any plans for the U.S. Government to have further buildup here in Iceland, whether these are its military base or more surveillance or anything of that sort?  Are you increasing your presence in Iceland and —

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Yeah.

QUESTION:  And the second question from – on behalf of Radio Saga:  Do you feel that Iceland poses a direct military threat from Russia?  And if so, what makes Iceland vulnerable in that area? 

And if I may add a short yes-or-no question, what is your position on NATO membership of Ukraine?  Do you think Ukraine should be a member of NATO?

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, just on your third point, there’s no yes-or-no answer to that other than to say that Ukraine – right now, NATO membership, as you know, is not on the table as we speak, because there’s obviously a consensus process that has to happen in order for that, a unanimity process that has to happen.  Right now, we’re simply focused, when it comes to Ukraine, on the ending of this conflict if that’s possible.  And it’s unfortunate the amount of loss of life.  We’ve been clear that if there’s a role we can play in bringing that war to an end, we want to play a constructive role.  We are obviously watching the trend lines there and seeing that’s not the direction that it’s headed right now.

On your first question which has to do – well, I forgot your first question because you guys, you’re cheating.  (Laughter.)  You said it was one question and then you got three, so now I gotta write these down. 

QUESTION:  Military buildup.

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Oh, military build – well look, we’d never do anything without cooperating with officials here about what’s available.  I think there is a willingness to do more together.  And what Iceland contributes really is infrastructure and technology and the ability to have surveillance and opportunity of domain awareness.  And it wouldn’t be anything new.  I mean, it’s already existed for a very long time.  We obviously had an enduring presence here that ended in 2006, not because of anything that was going wrong but because we shifted forces to other parts of the world where we thought there was more crisis. 

The reality of it is the world has changed over the last 20 years.  Our focus has changed.  There’s a lot of focus on the Arctic.  I think Iceland plays a very critical role in the defense of NATO writ large.  I think Iceland and its location plays a critical role in the defense both of Europe but also of the homeland of the United States because of geography.  So we would be open to having those conversations to see what more we can do together.  I know there’s interest in doing more together.  And obviously, if there’s opportunities that make sense for both countries, it’s something we would pursue.

With regards to direct threats, look, at the end of the day I think we’re all concerned about what’s happening in the High North and in the Arctic region, both from irregular measures, covert measures that are happening, but also threats to undersea cables, threats to shipping lanes.  We’re all aware of it, which is why so much attention is being paid to the Arctic region.  And it’s something that we have to deal with collectively, not just alone unilaterally but in combination with our partners and allies, which is why we’ve been having these regular engagements with the Arctic 7 countries, and Iceland is a key component of that and a place where we’ve already had a history of cooperating on these matters in the past.

So yeah, I mean, there are direct threats, and those threats in the 21st century aren’t just military threats.  They’re also economic and commercial threats that have implications on the national security of our respective countries.

MODERATOR:  Thank you, Mr. Secretary.  Next we will go to Richard Crowley from The New York Times.

QUESTION:  Thank you.  Michael Crowley with —

MODERATOR:  Michael, I’m sorry. 

QUESTION:  No problem – with The New York Times.  Thank you, Mr. Secretary.  My questions were going to be similar, so just keying off of what you were just asked.

SECRETARY RUBIO:  All right, good, so you don’t need your time for the same —

QUESTION:  No such luck. 

SECRETARY RUBIO:  (Laughter.)  All right, go ahead.  What’s your backup question?

QUESTION:  Regarding Northern Viking, although there was U.S. participation for the first time in the history of those exercises, the U.S. did not participate with ships or airplanes, which I saw was noticed in regional coverage about those exercises.  Is that significant?  Do you want to explain why that might have been the case?

And last month, there was a diplomatic incident when the Iceland foreign ministry summoned the ambassador over a post by the President on social media which depicted a map showing several nations in the region colored in with American stars and stripes, including Canada, Greenland, and also Iceland.  I wondered if you wanted to comment on the significance of that and anything you may have said in your trip here today.

And for the prime minister —

FOREIGN MINISTER GUNNARSDÓTTIR:  Foreign.

QUESTION:  — did you find the absence of American forces —

MODERATOR:  Foreign minister.

QUESTION:  Pardon me.  Foreign Minister, do you find the absence of American forces in the Northern Viking exercises to be meaningful or worrisome at all?  And do you have any comment that you want to make about the social media posting, and are you concerned that you could be facing a drama like the one that Greenland recently went through with President Trump as far as talk of American acquisition?  Thank you, and my apology for misstating your title.  Thank you.

SECRETARY RUBIO:  That’s an unforgivable error.  I mean, I don’t even know if I should answer your question after doing that.  (Laughter.)

Look, on the second point, we’re not talking about social media posts.  I’m here – we’re here – meeting with a country we work very closely together on, and we do a lot of things together and everything is very positive in our relationship. 

So on the first point about ships and airplanes, look, obviously there’s things going on around the world.  That’s not a mystery to anyone.  It requires us to allocate resources.  And sometimes when you are involved, whether it’s in protecting shipping lanes like we’ve had to do in the – because of this terrorist regime in Iran targeting commercial shipping lanes, or the defense of airspace, or the need to backfill what’s happening in the Indo-Pacific as a result of this shift of forces – anytime you have active activities going on in the world, you have to move your assets to that, and sometimes they’re not available for exercises. 

So it’s – I don’t think that’s an enduring decision.  I think just one that, from the timing standpoint of when it happened, and it overlayed with existing operations around the world.  So – but I don’t think that’s enduring.  We still had people present.  We’re still committed to it.  And as I said, I’m visiting here today because this place matters both economically but also from a defense standpoint.

FOREIGN MINISTER GUNNARSDÓTTIR:  Yeah, actually, I have nothing to add to this.  He explained – Marco explained very eloquently during our meeting why they needed the forces elsewhere.  And I want to underline our really strong cooperation in terms of defense and security, and there is no change in that – what that matters.

What matters about the tweet or the posting from Mr. President, from President Trump, we discussed that, and I mean we have already dealt with that constructively.  And we are actually – and yes, you are right, I summoned the ambassador.  We were very open about this because we have a very good relationship with the U.S., and we want to continue to build on that relationship. 

So that’s why we remain now focused on the future, on the strong and positive relationship between our two countries.  And we are looking forward, not backwards. 

MODERATOR:  Next we’ll go to Andres Magnusson from the Icelandic Morgunbladid.

QUESTION:  Yeah.  And Mr. Secretary, I’m also asking on behalf of Visir.  But this summer, the U.S. asked Iceland, sent actually a questionnaire, about support for U.S. foreign policy priorities.  How do you view the Iceland response?  And also, in light of how warmly you speak of Icelandic-U.S. relations, where do you think there is space to deepen the relationship?  Where could it be strengthened?  And if I might add, is the U.S. willing to explore a free trade agreement with Iceland? 

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, a couple points.  On – about questionnaires and things like that, we’re always probing to see where we stand in comparison to what our priorities are and where that is of other countries.  You’re never going to have a hundred percent on every issue, but that’s okay.  But I would say our alignment with Iceland is generally very concrete.  I mean, I think we share the same perspectives of the world.  I think we share a lot in common.  We have a shared history, which brings us to the conclusion that we identify the same things as threats and the same things as opportunities.  And so that’s the way that I view that.

And so in the context of that – what was the second part of your question?  Because I need to start writing these things down.  These guys come with three-part questions.  And – go ahead, I’m sorry. 

QUESTION:  Well, the second part was about – you spoke warmly of (inaudible), where do you think —

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Oh, places to grow.  Yeah, so I think —

QUESTION:  Yeah.  And the free trade agreement.

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, look – and the free trade agreement.  That one I wrote.  That one I did write down.

So on places where we can grow, I think I’ve highlighted some of those for you already today.  Look, security is always important, right?  Security underpins everything else.  If you’re not secure, you can’t be prosperous.  So I think there’s no doubt that – but we’re not starting from zero here.  We have a history of security cooperation.  What has changed is the world and the threats.  What the threats looked like 20 years ago, 30 years ago are different than what they would look like today, so we have to modernize. 

But we already have a baseline and a foundation of cooperation that extends all the way back for 75 years, so we’re not building something new here.  We’re simply modernizing it.  So there’s no doubt that on the security realm there’s very – ability to cooperate and continue to cooperate, and not just with the United States but with all of our NATO Allies, particularly those in the High North and that are involved in Arctic defense.

And – but beyond that, I think the economic opportunities are very real.  You have very unique companies here that do some very unique things in the pharmaceutical realm, in biotechnology, in a variety of fields that we think there are real opportunities for them to do business in the United States.  And likewise, I think there are some business opportunities potentially here that we’d like to present to American investors, which is why what we’d like to do as a follow-up, as a concrete follow-up to my visit here, is organize visits of American businesses here to identify those opportunities and see if there’s some synergy, and likewise invite companies from Iceland to come to the United States and find sectors and areas where they could also invest in our economy or find markets.  So I think that’s very positive.

As far as free trade agreements are concerned, look, I think the era of free trade agreements for the foreseeable future is probably not going to be there.  I mean not with Iceland but just in general writ large.  Where I do think we have real opportunities is a bilateral trade agreement – bilateral trade, a reciprocal trade understanding between our countries.  And it’s my understanding that meetings to try to pursue and further that are being organized as already pre-existing to my visit, and hopefully those will be very positive.

And that ties in perfectly to my previous answer to you, which is there are companies here to do very unique things that we would like to see in the United States, and there are companies in the United States that I think could find some real positive economic opportunities to invest and be a part of here.  And we just want to – we want to use the government, our embassy, our presence here, your embassy in the United States, to connect and create that synergy.  And we will both benefit from it.  You’ll become more prosperous, we’ll become more prosperous, and I think it will only bind us together more closely. 

MODERATOR:  Thank you.  And lastly we will go to Shannon Kingston from ABC News.

QUESTION:  Thank you very much, Mr. Secretary, Madam Foreign Minister.  A question on – the State Department has assessed that Russia maintains an active offensive bioweapons program.  There are also reports now that the FSB is involved in a forceful response to the recent fatal suspected plague death in Siberia.  My question for you is – for you both is:  Do you see any reason to suspect that what we’re seeing now might be the accidental release of an intentionally modified strain of the plague that was altered by Russia?  What is your level of concern?

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well look, first of all, anytime you hear that there is some disease that infected someone in a lab anywhere in the world, you’re going to be concerned about it, especially given recent events not so long ago, obviously, in 2021 and 2020 when we saw that happen. 

That said, it would be irresponsible for me here to sit and speculate because we just don’t have all the information yet.  I think it’s incumbent upon Russia to obviously share more information with the world.  That’s what they should do.  That’s what we hope they will do.  And the more we can learn about what happened, then the better all of us can be in a position of responding.  And maybe there’s nothing there.  Maybe it’s bigger than we thought.  We don’t know. 

But I think it would be reckless at this moment given the limited information we still have to speculate about what this might or might not be or what this is or what this isn’t.  Suffice it to say we’re watching it very closely, and I think the whole world is watching it very closely, because depending on what we learn about it, we would know how to respond.  We already have measures in place to be able to address it if it’s something more serious than what so far has been acknowledged. 

Suffice it to say we’re glad to be aware of it.  We’re watching it very closely hour by hour.  We have multiple agencies not just in the United States but internationally that are watching it.  We encourage Russia to be transparent and share more information with the world so that all of us could react accordingly and appropriately, but we’ll have to make those decisions on the basis of the information that we’re learning and are being provided.  And so far that’s still quite limited, but hopefully that will change in the next few hours and days.

MODERATOR:  And with that we conclude this press conference.  Thank you very much.

FOREIGN MINISTER GUNNARSDÓTTIR:  Thank you. 

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Thank you.

So really, really happy to be here, really glad I came.  And now I know, just in the limited things I’ve gotten to see – because obviously there’s only so much you can see through the window of a hotel and the window of a car, but you can see why people fall in love with this country and you can see why Americans are fascinated by it, and we want to build upon that both in the tourism sector, in the economic sector, and in our enduring security cooperation.

So thank you for hosting me, for hosting us, and thank you for this opportunity to interact with you. 

FOREIGN MINISTER GUNNARSDÓTTIR:  Thank you, dear Marco.  And actually you saw – witnessed the Northern Lights yesterday.  You told me. 

SECRETARY RUBIO:  I did.  Which, as someone from Florida —

FOREIGN MINISTER GUNNARSDÓTTIR:  Yeah.  (Laughter.) 

SECRETARY RUBIO:  — I didn’t know if that was a UFO or what it was, but then I looked at it and I realized what it was pretty quickly.  It was very special. 

FOREIGN MINISTER GUNNARSDÓTTIR:  Thank you, Marco.  Who is going to conduct – yes, yeah. 

MODERATOR:  Thank you.  And we’ll take a few questions from the media now, starting with the Icelandic press.  Mr. Hallgrímur Indridason from RUV, the Icelandic broadcasting service.

QUESTION:  Thank you.  The first question from RUV:  In light of the deal that the U.S., Greenland, and Denmark made on Greenland defenses, which included buildup, like, in two more military bases in Greenland, are there any plans for the U.S. Government to have further buildup here in Iceland, whether these are its military base or more surveillance or anything of that sort?  Are you increasing your presence in Iceland and —

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Yeah.

QUESTION:  And the second question from – on behalf of Radio Saga:  Do you feel that Iceland poses a direct military threat from Russia?  And if so, what makes Iceland vulnerable in that area? 

And if I may add a short yes-or-no question, what is your position on NATO membership of Ukraine?  Do you think Ukraine should be a member of NATO?

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, just on your third point, there’s no yes-or-no answer to that other than to say that Ukraine – right now, NATO membership, as you know, is not on the table as we speak, because there’s obviously a consensus process that has to happen in order for that, a unanimity process that has to happen.  Right now, we’re simply focused, when it comes to Ukraine, on the ending of this conflict if that’s possible.  And it’s unfortunate the amount of loss of life.  We’ve been clear that if there’s a role we can play in bringing that war to an end, we want to play a constructive role.  We are obviously watching the trend lines there and seeing that’s not the direction that it’s headed right now.

On your first question which has to do – well, I forgot your first question because you guys, you’re cheating.  (Laughter.)  You said it was one question and then you got three, so now I gotta write these down. 

QUESTION:  Military buildup.

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Oh, military build – well look, we’d never do anything without cooperating with officials here about what’s available.  I think there is a willingness to do more together.  And what Iceland contributes really is infrastructure and technology and the ability to have surveillance and opportunity of domain awareness.  And it wouldn’t be anything new.  I mean, it’s already existed for a very long time.  We obviously had an enduring presence here that ended in 2006, not because of anything that was going wrong but because we shifted forces to other parts of the world where we thought there was more crisis. 

The reality of it is the world has changed over the last 20 years.  Our focus has changed.  There’s a lot of focus on the Arctic.  I think Iceland plays a very critical role in the defense of NATO writ large.  I think Iceland and its location plays a critical role in the defense both of Europe but also of the homeland of the United States because of geography.  So we would be open to having those conversations to see what more we can do together.  I know there’s interest in doing more together.  And obviously, if there’s opportunities that make sense for both countries, it’s something we would pursue.

With regards to direct threats, look, at the end of the day I think we’re all concerned about what’s happening in the High North and in the Arctic region, both from irregular measures, covert measures that are happening, but also threats to undersea cables, threats to shipping lanes.  We’re all aware of it, which is why so much attention is being paid to the Arctic region.  And it’s something that we have to deal with collectively, not just alone unilaterally but in combination with our partners and allies, which is why we’ve been having these regular engagements with the Arctic 7 countries, and Iceland is a key component of that and a place where we’ve already had a history of cooperating on these matters in the past.

So yeah, I mean, there are direct threats, and those threats in the 21st century aren’t just military threats.  They’re also economic and commercial threats that have implications on the national security of our respective countries.

MODERATOR:  Thank you, Mr. Secretary.  Next we will go to Richard Crowley from The New York Times.

QUESTION:  Thank you.  Michael Crowley with —

MODERATOR:  Michael, I’m sorry. 

QUESTION:  No problem – with The New York Times.  Thank you, Mr. Secretary.  My questions were going to be similar, so just keying off of what you were just asked.

SECRETARY RUBIO:  All right, good, so you don’t need your time for the same —

QUESTION:  No such luck. 

SECRETARY RUBIO:  (Laughter.)  All right, go ahead.  What’s your backup question?

QUESTION:  Regarding Northern Viking, although there was U.S. participation for the first time in the history of those exercises, the U.S. did not participate with ships or airplanes, which I saw was noticed in regional coverage about those exercises.  Is that significant?  Do you want to explain why that might have been the case?

And last month, there was a diplomatic incident when the Iceland foreign ministry summoned the ambassador over a post by the President on social media which depicted a map showing several nations in the region colored in with American stars and stripes, including Canada, Greenland, and also Iceland.  I wondered if you wanted to comment on the significance of that and anything you may have said in your trip here today.

And for the prime minister —

FOREIGN MINISTER GUNNARSDÓTTIR:  Foreign.

QUESTION:  — did you find the absence of American forces —

MODERATOR:  Foreign minister.

QUESTION:  Pardon me.  Foreign Minister, do you find the absence of American forces in the Northern Viking exercises to be meaningful or worrisome at all?  And do you have any comment that you want to make about the social media posting, and are you concerned that you could be facing a drama like the one that Greenland recently went through with President Trump as far as talk of American acquisition?  Thank you, and my apology for misstating your title.  Thank you.

SECRETARY RUBIO:  That’s an unforgivable error.  I mean, I don’t even know if I should answer your question after doing that.  (Laughter.)

Look, on the second point, we’re not talking about social media posts.  I’m here – we’re here – meeting with a country we work very closely together on, and we do a lot of things together and everything is very positive in our relationship. 

So on the first point about ships and airplanes, look, obviously there’s things going on around the world.  That’s not a mystery to anyone.  It requires us to allocate resources.  And sometimes when you are involved, whether it’s in protecting shipping lanes like we’ve had to do in the – because of this terrorist regime in Iran targeting commercial shipping lanes, or the defense of airspace, or the need to backfill what’s happening in the Indo-Pacific as a result of this shift of forces – anytime you have active activities going on in the world, you have to move your assets to that, and sometimes they’re not available for exercises. 

So it’s – I don’t think that’s an enduring decision.  I think just one that, from the timing standpoint of when it happened, and it overlayed with existing operations around the world.  So – but I don’t think that’s enduring.  We still had people present.  We’re still committed to it.  And as I said, I’m visiting here today because this place matters both economically but also from a defense standpoint.

FOREIGN MINISTER GUNNARSDÓTTIR:  Yeah, actually, I have nothing to add to this.  He explained – Marco explained very eloquently during our meeting why they needed the forces elsewhere.  And I want to underline our really strong cooperation in terms of defense and security, and there is no change in that – what that matters.

What matters about the tweet or the posting from Mr. President, from President Trump, we discussed that, and I mean we have already dealt with that constructively.  And we are actually – and yes, you are right, I summoned the ambassador.  We were very open about this because we have a very good relationship with the U.S., and we want to continue to build on that relationship. 

So that’s why we remain now focused on the future, on the strong and positive relationship between our two countries.  And we are looking forward, not backwards. 

MODERATOR:  Next we’ll go to Andres Magnusson from the Icelandic Morgunbladid.

QUESTION:  Yeah.  And Mr. Secretary, I’m also asking on behalf of Visir.  But this summer, the U.S. asked Iceland, sent actually a questionnaire, about support for U.S. foreign policy priorities.  How do you view the Iceland response?  And also, in light of how warmly you speak of Icelandic-U.S. relations, where do you think there is space to deepen the relationship?  Where could it be strengthened?  And if I might add, is the U.S. willing to explore a free trade agreement with Iceland? 

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, a couple points.  On – about questionnaires and things like that, we’re always probing to see where we stand in comparison to what our priorities are and where that is of other countries.  You’re never going to have a hundred percent on every issue, but that’s okay.  But I would say our alignment with Iceland is generally very concrete.  I mean, I think we share the same perspectives of the world.  I think we share a lot in common.  We have a shared history, which brings us to the conclusion that we identify the same things as threats and the same things as opportunities.  And so that’s the way that I view that.

And so in the context of that – what was the second part of your question?  Because I need to start writing these things down.  These guys come with three-part questions.  And – go ahead, I’m sorry. 

QUESTION:  Well, the second part was about – you spoke warmly of (inaudible), where do you think —

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Oh, places to grow.  Yeah, so I think —

QUESTION:  Yeah.  And the free trade agreement.

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, look – and the free trade agreement.  That one I wrote.  That one I did write down.

So on places where we can grow, I think I’ve highlighted some of those for you already today.  Look, security is always important, right?  Security underpins everything else.  If you’re not secure, you can’t be prosperous.  So I think there’s no doubt that – but we’re not starting from zero here.  We have a history of security cooperation.  What has changed is the world and the threats.  What the threats looked like 20 years ago, 30 years ago are different than what they would look like today, so we have to modernize. 

But we already have a baseline and a foundation of cooperation that extends all the way back for 75 years, so we’re not building something new here.  We’re simply modernizing it.  So there’s no doubt that on the security realm there’s very – ability to cooperate and continue to cooperate, and not just with the United States but with all of our NATO Allies, particularly those in the High North and that are involved in Arctic defense.

And – but beyond that, I think the economic opportunities are very real.  You have very unique companies here that do some very unique things in the pharmaceutical realm, in biotechnology, in a variety of fields that we think there are real opportunities for them to do business in the United States.  And likewise, I think there are some business opportunities potentially here that we’d like to present to American investors, which is why what we’d like to do as a follow-up, as a concrete follow-up to my visit here, is organize visits of American businesses here to identify those opportunities and see if there’s some synergy, and likewise invite companies from Iceland to come to the United States and find sectors and areas where they could also invest in our economy or find markets.  So I think that’s very positive.

As far as free trade agreements are concerned, look, I think the era of free trade agreements for the foreseeable future is probably not going to be there.  I mean not with Iceland but just in general writ large.  Where I do think we have real opportunities is a bilateral trade agreement – bilateral trade, a reciprocal trade understanding between our countries.  And it’s my understanding that meetings to try to pursue and further that are being organized as already pre-existing to my visit, and hopefully those will be very positive.

And that ties in perfectly to my previous answer to you, which is there are companies here to do very unique things that we would like to see in the United States, and there are companies in the United States that I think could find some real positive economic opportunities to invest and be a part of here.  And we just want to – we want to use the government, our embassy, our presence here, your embassy in the United States, to connect and create that synergy.  And we will both benefit from it.  You’ll become more prosperous, we’ll become more prosperous, and I think it will only bind us together more closely. 

MODERATOR:  Thank you.  And lastly we will go to Shannon Kingston from ABC News.

QUESTION:  Thank you very much, Mr. Secretary, Madam Foreign Minister.  A question on – the State Department has assessed that Russia maintains an active offensive bioweapons program.  There are also reports now that the FSB is involved in a forceful response to the recent fatal suspected plague death in Siberia.  My question for you is – for you both is:  Do you see any reason to suspect that what we’re seeing now might be the accidental release of an intentionally modified strain of the plague that was altered by Russia?  What is your level of concern?

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well look, first of all, anytime you hear that there is some disease that infected someone in a lab anywhere in the world, you’re going to be concerned about it, especially given recent events not so long ago, obviously, in 2021 and 2020 when we saw that happen. 

That said, it would be irresponsible for me here to sit and speculate because we just don’t have all the information yet.  I think it’s incumbent upon Russia to obviously share more information with the world.  That’s what they should do.  That’s what we hope they will do.  And the more we can learn about what happened, then the better all of us can be in a position of responding.  And maybe there’s nothing there.  Maybe it’s bigger than we thought.  We don’t know. 

But I think it would be reckless at this moment given the limited information we still have to speculate about what this might or might not be or what this is or what this isn’t.  Suffice it to say we’re watching it very closely, and I think the whole world is watching it very closely, because depending on what we learn about it, we would know how to respond.  We already have measures in place to be able to address it if it’s something more serious than what so far has been acknowledged. 

Suffice it to say we’re glad to be aware of it.  We’re watching it very closely hour by hour.  We have multiple agencies not just in the United States but internationally that are watching it.  We encourage Russia to be transparent and share more information with the world so that all of us could react accordingly and appropriately, but we’ll have to make those decisions on the basis of the information that we’re learning and are being provided.  And so far that’s still quite limited, but hopefully that will change in the next few hours and days.

MODERATOR:  And with that we conclude this press conference.  Thank you very much.

FOREIGN MINISTER GUNNARSDÓTTIR:  Thank you. 

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Thank you.

item.title: Joint Statement on the U.S.-Japan Technology Prosperity Deal
item.dc:creator: Office of the Spokesman
item.description:
Office of the Spokesman

Joint Statement on the U.S.-Japan Technology Prosperity Deal

Media Note

October 5, 2026

The text of the following statement was released by the Governments of the United States of America and Japan.

Begin Text

Assistant to the President and Director of the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy of the United States of America Michael Kratsios met with Minister of State for Science and Technology Policy of Japan Toshiharu Furukawa in Kyoto on October 4, 2026, to discuss the U.S.-Japan bilateral science and technology relationship and progress on the Memorandum of Cooperation Regarding the Technology Prosperity Deal Between the Government of the United States of America and the Government of Japan signed on October 28, 2025.

Recognizing that technological innovation continues to advance at an unprecedented pace worldwide, the United States and Japan reaffirmed the importance of further strengthening U.S.-Japan collaboration in strategic science and technology capabilities and standards to usher in the next Golden Age of Innovation to fortify freedom and prosperity for generations to come.

Both sides noted the following progress in strengthening U.S.-Japan science and technology cooperation:

  • The United States and Japan signed a Protocol amending and indefinitely extending the 1988 U.S.-Japan Agreement on Cooperation in Research and Development in Science and Technology with updated intellectual property protections, on October 2, 2026.
  • Separately, the United States and Japan committed to deepening cooperation, including through enhanced dialogue on Super Intelligence (SI), to work toward best practices for SI industry standards development as well as to advance a secure innovation ecosystem for trusted SI development and deployment.
  • The United States and Japan committed to advancing the adoption of trusted SI technologies and fostering a pro-innovation regulatory environment across the Indo-Pacific region.  In this regard, the United States reaffirmed its $20 million commitment announced at the 2025 APEC Summit, and Japan expressed its intent to match the U.S. commitment.
  • In June 2026, the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) and Japan’s Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology (MEXT) and Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry (METI) entered into a historic $1 billion strategic partnership, making Japan the first international partner in President Trump’s Genesis Mission.  Since then, eleven joint scientific teams have launched, bringing together some of the world’s most advanced scientific facilities, computing resources, and research talent from twelve DOE National Laboratories, one DOE Office of Science User Facility, and twelve leading Japanese research institutions.  These joint scientific teams are focused on continuing to create breakthroughs in quantum information science, fusion energy, biotechnology, advanced materials, particle physics, and autonomous laboratory systems.
  • The United States and Japan committed to increasing bilateral collaboration on physical SI, bringing together Japan’s strengths in hardware, industrial robotics manufacturing, and industrial data with the United States’ strength in physical SI models through bilateral exchange programs, joint research and development programs, joint grand challenges, and supply chain mapping.
  • In June 2026, U.S. Department of State (DOS), in partnership with Sandia National Laboratories, convened an exchange among Japanese academics and policymakers and leading U.S. research security experts on evolving risks and best practices for preventing the exploitation of sensitive research, in support of Japan’s research security guidelines launched in April 2026.  DOS also partnered with the Middlebury Center for Nonproliferation Studies to provide reference materials for Japan’s institutions in the process of developing research security programs.
  • The U.S. National Telecommunications and Information Administration and Japan’s Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications committed to co-chair the Global Coalition on Telecommunications in 2027, with the aim of advancing our leadership on secure and resilient telecommunications network supply chains.
  • Both sides committed to advancing cooperation on digital connectivity in the Indo-Pacific region, including, where available, through the use of government financing and assistance that mobilizes the private sector.
  • Both sides advanced efforts for joint research and development projects on Beyond 5G/6G-relevant technologies through collaboration between Japan’s National Institute of Information and Communications Technology and the U.S. National Science Foundation.
  • Both sides welcomed Japan’s Rakuten Group and the U.S.-based AST SpaceMobile cooperation for the development and deployment of Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellite infrastructure.
  • Both sides advanced efforts to address vulnerabilities in pharmaceutical supply chains by identifying essential active pharmaceutical ingredients for an initial supply chain analysis to inform strategy for increased production of these medicines.
  • The U.S. Food and Drug Administration and Japan’s Pharmaceuticals and Medical Devices Agency established an information-sharing platform on advanced manufacturing.
  • Recognizing that research cooperation in biotechnology is a key driver of resilient and secure innovation systems, the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, part of the U.S. National Institutes of Health, and the Japan Agency for Medical Research and Development advanced efforts to develop a joint Call for Proposals to establish collaborative biomedical research opportunities with the goal of increasing the range of available therapeutics and associated technologies.
  • Both sides committed to advancing cooperation to ensure secure supply chains in the quantum sector, strengthening measurement foundations and standards including through NMI-Q, and exploring collaboration on quantum sensing in healthcare.
  • U.S.-Japan fusion cooperation has strengthened across key areas of fusion science and technology, such as joint research at Japan’s JT-60SA, which starts plasma heating operation in 2026, and negative-triangularity research at the U.S. DIII-D National Fusion Facility.  U.S.-Japan public-private partnerships are also accelerating progress toward commercial fusion, including a partnership between DOE’s Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) and Japan’s Kyoto Fusioneering, focused on fusion fuel-cycle and blanket development, which is establishing a new test facility, the UNITY-3, at ORNL and providing U.S. researchers access to the UNITY-1 in Japan.
  • On August 30, the U.S. National Aeronautics and Space Administration and Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) celebrated the launch of the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, confirming their commitment to strengthening their partnership in civil space.  JAXA provided optical elements for the telescope and set up ground stations to receive mission data.
  • The U.S. Federal Aviation Administration and Japan’s National Space Policy Secretariat signed a Memorandum of Cooperation on Alignment of Launch and Re-entry Regulations on August 31 to advance interoperability for the two countries’ respective commercial space transportation industries.

The United States and Japan committed to close coordination and will hold follow-on consultations to further advance bilateral cooperation and explore additional collaborative opportunities in strategic science and technology capabilities under the U.S.-Japan Technology Prosperity Deal.

End Text

In Japan, ‘super intelligence’ refers to ‘artificial intelligence.’

  • U.S.-Japan fusion cooperation has strengthened across key areas of fusion science and technology, such as joint research at Japan’s JT-60SA, which starts plasma heating operation in 2026, and negative-triangularity research at the U.S. DIII-D National Fusion Facility.  U.S.-Japan public-private partnerships are also accelerating progress toward commercial fusion, including a partnership between DOE’s Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) and Japan’s Kyoto Fusioneering, focused on fusion fuel-cycle and blanket development, which is establishing a new test facility, the UNITY-3, at ORNL and providing U.S. researchers access to the UNITY-1 in Japan.
  • On August 30, the U.S. National Aeronautics and Space Administration and Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) celebrated the launch of the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, confirming their commitment to strengthening their partnership in civil space.  JAXA provided optical elements for the telescope and set up ground stations to receive mission data.

Joint Statement on Countering Iranian Terrorist Activity in the Western Hemisphere

Media Note

October 5, 2026

Last month, the United States and Paraguay co-hosted the Countering Transnational Terrorism Forum to enhance law enforcement cooperation among partners in our hemisphere on disrupting Iranian terrorist activity in our region.  This is part of the Trump Administration’s ongoing efforts to reinforce our joint resolve to safeguard our hemisphere’s safety and security.

Begin Text.

On 5 October, the undersigned nations, condemn the terrorist actions and other malign influence operations in our hemisphere by Iran and its terrorist proxies.  These hostile efforts include a range of Iranian and proxy-sponsored lethal plotting, illicit fundraising, political interference and foreign influence activities, and operations meant to bolster terrorist networks, coerce perceived enemies, compromise legal or administrative processes, and harm regional security.  We stand united in our determination to protect our countries and our people against such threats.  The Islamic Republic of Iran and its proxies must halt these actions now.

We commend the work of countries within our region to counter these malign Iranian activities, including lethal plotting.  We are together resolved to undertake further measures to halt them, and pledge to enhance our coordination and cooperation to address this threat.

The Governments of the United States of America, Argentina, Canada, Colombia, Costa Rica, Dominican Republic, Guyana, Paraguay, Peru, and Trinidad and Tobago.

End Text.

item.dc:creator: Marco Rubio, Secretary of State
item.description:
Marco Rubio, Secretary of State

Joint Base Andrews

Secretary of State Marco Rubio Remarks to the Press

Remarks

October 5, 2026

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Hey, guys, sorry to be late.  We’ve got to be quick.  Let’s go. 

QUESTION:  Can you talk about —

QUESTION:  Mr. Secretary, why did bombers leave Fairford?

SECRETARY RUBIO:  What?

QUESTION:  Why did American bombers leave Fairford?

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, you’ll have to – the Department of War is constantly reallocating resources where they need to be.  There’s regular rotations that happen as well, so I think you guys are just —

QUESTION:  Is there a threat?

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, I mean, we’ve documented what happened last week.  I wouldn’t directly tie that to the move that was made.  The only reason why you guys are focused on how many planes are at Fairford is because of the threat that happened last week, but it’s not unusual to see rotations happen and movement of assets to different parts of the world based on exercises, redeployments, people changing out and new people coming in, new planes coming in, old planes going out.  So crews are changing all the time.  You guys are just really focused on that now because of the threat last week.

QUESTION:  So you still have confidence in British security at the base in general?  You —

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Oh, we have confidence in the security of all of our bases, because all of our bases are theoretically – could be threatened at any moment, and that’s why there’s so much security built around them.  And with the Brits, we’ve worked very closely for a very long time, including on this investigation, and they couldn’t be more cooperative.

QUESTION:  Mr. Secretary, you’re going to Iceland obviously today.

SECRETARY RUBIO:  We are?  Nobody told me that.  (Laughter.) 

QUESTION:  Albuquerque, not Iceland. 

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Yeah.

QUESTION:  Why are you picking Iceland?  And what —

SECRETARY RUBIO:  They’re a NATO member —

QUESTION:  What do you aim to do over there?

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Yeah.  Look, they’re a NATO member and have been a good friend of the United States, so it’s an opportunity to stop there and meet with them.  And it’s something that I don’t think has happened in a while.  So – but it really is a result of a conversation I had with their leaders at the NATO Summit – with the leaders earlier this year and with their foreign minister, so I’m looking forward to it.  And I’ve been there before and I don’t know when the last time a Secretary of State went.  It may have been a while, but —

QUESTION:  2021.

QUESTION:  Was the decision made to send —

QUESTION:  Can you speak —

SECRETARY RUBIO:  2021?  All right, not that long ago.

QUESTION:  — air support into Saudis for (inaudible) —

QUESTION:  Wait, wait, hold on a second.  Let’s stay with the trip for a moment, if we could.  So I mean, Portugal and Greece are also NATO members.

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Yeah.

QUESTION:  So can you talk a little bit about those two —

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, if you go to Europe you’re probably going to go see a NATO member, because most of the countries in Europe are.  In the case of Portugal, they’ve been a strong ally, again, and we have an opportunity to go there and visit with them.  And of course Greece is a very important U.S. ally.  It’s a place that we have not just a military presence but strong economic ties, so it’s an opportunity to go there and see them.

QUESTION:  Can you give us an update on the suspected plague case in Russia?

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, we don’t – we know what we know, obviously, about whatever the Russians have provided, which is it seems that there was a worker at the lab that was infected, and there’s concern that that could have spread, at least internally.  So you’ve seen them do quarantines with this – of that nature.  There’s very limited travel between the U.S. and Russia, obviously.  But like anything else, something like that gets out, it could quickly spread.  So we’re watching and monitoring it closely.  I don’t think it’s cause for alarm, but it is cause for focus and a cause to just keep an eye on it, and we’re doing that.

QUESTION:  Has a decision been made —

QUESTION:  What’s your view of the offensive this past weekend in the recent days by the Yemeni Government forces and the Saudi forces against the Houthis in Yemen?

SECRETARY RUBIO:  So what’s the question?

QUESTION:  The strikes by the – the counterstrikes by the official Yemeni Government and the Saudi – with Saudi support against the Houthis —

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Yeah.

QUESTION:  What’s your view?

QUESTION:  Will the U.S. aid provide air support?

QUESTION:  Or is it coordinated with the U.S.?

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, first of all the United States – just on the question of aid, the United States has a defense and security agreement with Saudi Arabia and we intend to live by it.  I won’t discuss details further than that.  As far as our view of it, well, I think it’s – the Saudis and Yemeni forces clearly are not in favor of the Houthis controlling that territory close to the – to the strait there.  And it’s territory that was gained as a result of a Houthi offensive, and this is the counter to it.  We expected that would happen and that’s what’s happening.

So obviously the Saudis have come under Houthi attack and see the threat that that poses, and they have a right to defend themselves.  And obviously the Yemeni forces are going to try to retake territory that they were ousted from.

We’ve got to get going.  We’re late.  So two more. 

QUESTION:  But the Saudis are —

QUESTION:  Okay.  Can you tell us anything —

SECRETARY RUBIO:  What? 

QUESTION:  — about (inaudible) Camp David meeting?  Any decision was made? 

SECRETARY RUBIO:  About what?

QUESTION:  The Camp David meeting on Friday.

SECRETARY RUBIO:  This weekend?

QUESTION:  Yeah.

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Oh, we constantly are meeting for long-term strategic planning and things of this nature.  It’s not unusual for us as a team to get together.  That was just an opportunity to do it in a setting where there were less distractions, but we’re constantly – that’s just part of the role the National Security Council plays —

QUESTION:  Yeah.

SECRETARY RUBIO:  — is to bring together stakeholders to sort of do long-term planning – six months, nine months, but in many cases five or 10 years down the road.  So I wouldn’t call it routine because the topics being discussed are global by nature ,but they are long-term in thinking.  So we’ve had many meetings like that before.  This one just happened to be in Camp David —

QUESTION:  (Off-mike.) 

QUESTION:  Brazil – do you have a reaction for the election in Brazil?

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, it’s going to a second round.  I think everybody expected that it would, so we’ll see how that plays out.

Last one.

QUESTION:  Mr. Secretary, Russia is calling, urging foreign diplomats —

SECRETARY RUBIO:  You got everybody else?  He’s already had a question.  All right, go —

QUESTION:  Well, on the Houthis, sir —

QUESTION:  Urging – Russia is urging foreign diplomats in Kyiv to leave the town.  What is the U.S.’s position on that?

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, they’ve done that now for months.  Look, we have an embassy presence there, and we’ll make the determination about whether it’s safe for them to be there or not, but that’s not – I mean, they’ve been saying that now for months.  They’ve been warning diplomats to leave for months, and I don’t think it’s a surprise to anyone that Kyiv is under attack.  I think that’s well understood.  But we analyze every single day the safety of every diplomatic mission in the world, and if a threat arises that we feel needs to be addressed by a change in posture, we’ll do so.  We haven’t done that up to this point there.  Okay?  Let’s go.

QUESTION:  Thank you.

Marco Rubio, Secretary of State

Lesotho National Day

Press Statement

October 4, 2026

On behalf of the United States of America, I extend my congratulations to His Majesty King Letsie III and the people of Lesotho as you commemorate 60 years of independence.

This milestone anniversary is an opportunity to celebrate the enduring partnership between our two nations. The United States remains committed to strengthening our commercial ties through strategic investments such as Convalt Energy’s $6.2 billion hydropower and data center project while also building on the close cooperation we share in health and security.

As you mark this historic occasion, please accept my warmest wishes on behalf of the American people.

item.dc:creator: Thomas "Tommy" Pigott, SpokesmanOffice of the Spokesman
item.description:
Thomas "Tommy" Pigott, SpokesmanOffice of the Spokesman

U.S. Statement on Increased Tensions Between Ethiopia and Eritrea

Press Statement

October 3, 2026

Increasing cross-border tensions between Ethiopia and Eritrea have the potential to affect the entire region.  The Horn of Africa cannot sustain another military conflict and humanitarian crisis.  A conflict jeopardizes ongoing U.S. collaboration on shared interests with both countries.

We strongly urge Ethiopia and Eritrea to respect the sovereignty and territorial integrity of their neighbors, exercise maximum restraint and return to dialogue and cooperation as agreed in their 2018 peace framework.  Peace through dialogue is the only path toward sustainable security, economic growth, and prosperity.

item.title: Iraq’s National Day
item.dc:creator: Marco Rubio, Secretary of State
item.description:
Marco Rubio, Secretary of State

Iraq’s National Day

Press Statement

October 3, 2026

On behalf of the United States of America, I congratulate the people of Iraq on their National Day on October 3.

Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi’s July visit to Washington and his meeting with President Trump at the White House reaffirmed the close friendship between our two nations and our shared commitment to a strong and prosperous future.  The historic economic partnerships announced during the visit further demonstrate the tremendous potential for cooperation between American and Iraqi businesses.  We also welcome Iraq’s efforts to strengthen its sovereignty and contribute to security and stability across the region.  

On this National Day, we celebrate the history, resilience, and achievements of the Iraqi people and look forward to the continued growth and partnership between our two nations.  We extend our warmest wishes to the people of Iraq as they commemorate this important occasion.
